solutions: Use logical clocks for causal ordering

When you need a consistent ordering that never violates cause-and-effect but do not need real time, use Lamport timestamps: a per-process counter, incremented before each event and advanced to `max(local, received) + 1` on receive. This guarantees the Clock Condition (`a -> b` implies `C(a) < C(b)`) with no hardware clock at all. Break ties by process ID when you need a stable total order across all nodes — accepting that the tiebreak is a convention imposed on concurrent events, not a real precedence.
Use vector clocks when you need to DETECT concurrency

Lamport clocks are one-directional: `C(a) < C(b)` does not tell you whether a happened-before b or the two are concurrent. If your system must distinguish causal dependence from concurrency — e.g. detecting conflicting writes in a replicated store or driving causal consistency — use vector clocks (one counter per process). Comparing two vectors tells you exactly whether one happened-before the other or whether they are concurrent, which is precisely the information Lamport timestamps discard.
Use bounded-uncertainty physical clocks (Spanner TrueTime) when you truly need wall-clock order

If you genuinely need externally-consistent real-time ordering (e.g. a globally distributed database that must order transactions by real time), do not trust a bare timestamp comparison. Use an infrastructure like Google Spanner's TrueTime, which gives each node a bounded uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` from GPS and atomic clocks, and then WAITS OUT that interval before committing so no later transaction can be stamped earlier. This manages the uncertainty at a real latency cost — it does not eliminate it.
Never assume synchronized clocks across nodes

Treat any cross-host wall-clock comparison as suspect by default. NTP leaves an unknown residual error and clocks drift continuously, so two timestamps from two machines within that error window can be ordered backwards. Do not use raw `currentTimeMillis()` comparisons to decide which distributed event came first, to expire leases, or to resolve write conflicts. If a decision depends on ordering across hosts, base it on causality (logical/vector clocks) or on bounded-uncertainty time — never on the naive assumption that clocks agree.
topics.papers: Leslie Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System," Communications of the ACM 21(7), 1978 — origin of the happened-before relation (->), the Clock Condition, logical clocks as pure counters, and the Lamport timestamp algorithm; establishes that happened-before is only a partial order because concurrent events cannot be ordered. Caveat on the absolute framing: Google Spanner's TrueTime (Corbett et al., "Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database," OSDI 2012) uses GPS and atomic clocks to bound clock uncertainty and commit-waits out the uncertainty interval to achieve external ordering — an engineering workaround that manages, rather than refutes, Lamport's point that physical clocks alone cannot order distributed events. Vector clocks (Fidge/Mattern, 1988) extend Lamport clocks to capture causality exactly, distinguishing causal dependence from true concurrency.
topics.takeaway: Across the network there is no shared clock and messages take real time, so wall-clock timestamps can order events backwards — only causality is well-defined, and causality is only ever a partial order. Track it with logical or vector clocks; if you truly need real-time order, bound the clock uncertainty and wait it out.

mcqs.q: Under Lamport's happened-before relation (->), which of the following establishes that event a happened before event b?
options: a's physical clock reads an earlier time than b's physical clock
a is the sending of a message and b is the receipt of that same message
a and b occur on different machines that are geographically far apart
a and b were both timestamped within the same NTP synchronization window
mcqs.explanation: Happened-before is defined without physical clocks. Its rules are: same-process precedence, message send-before-receive, and transitivity. A send preceding its matching receive is exactly rule (2). Physical clock readings, geography, and NTP windows are irrelevant to the definition.

mcqs.q: Why is happened-before described as only a PARTIAL order rather than a total order?
options: Because clocks are imperfect, so we can never measure the true total order but it still exists
Because there exist concurrent events — pairs with neither a->b nor b->a — that genuinely cannot be ordered
Because message delays make ordering slow to compute, not impossible
Because process IDs are needed to break ties before any order exists at all
mcqs.explanation: Lamport states it is sometimes impossible to say which of two events occurred first: concurrent events have no causal path either way, so there is genuinely no fact about their order. This is a real absence of comparability, not a measurement limitation or a performance issue.

mcqs.q: In the Lamport timestamp algorithm, what does a process do to its counter when it RECEIVES a message carrying timestamp t?
options: Sets the counter to t exactly, adopting the sender's clock
Increments its own counter by one and ignores t
Sets the counter to max(local, t) + 1
Averages its local counter with t to converge the two clocks
mcqs.explanation: On receive, the counter becomes max(local, received) + 1. The max drags the receiver's clock past the sender's, and the +1 guarantees the receive event gets a strictly larger value than the matching send, enforcing the Clock Condition.

mcqs.q: What can you conclude if you observe that two events have Lamport timestamps C(a) < C(b)?
options: That a definitely happened before b
That a and b are definitely concurrent
Nothing about causality by itself — a may have happened before b, or they may be concurrent
That b definitely happened before a
mcqs.explanation: Lamport clocks are one-directional: a->b implies C(a)<C(b), but the converse does not hold. A smaller timestamp is consistent with either a->b or with a and b being concurrent, so it cannot by itself establish causality.

mcqs.q: What capability do vector clocks provide that Lamport (scalar) clocks do not?
options: They keep physical time accurate without GPS or atomic clocks
They eliminate message delay so ordering becomes instantaneous
They can determine exactly whether two events are causally related or genuinely concurrent
They remove the need for any per-event counter increment
mcqs.explanation: Vector clocks (one counter per process) capture causality exactly: comparing two vectors tells you definitively whether one happened-before the other or whether they are concurrent — the distinction that scalar Lamport timestamps discard. They do not address physical time or network delay.

mcqs.q: How does Google Spanner's TrueTime relate to Lamport's claim that physical clocks cannot order distributed events?
options: It refutes Lamport by proving perfectly synchronized clocks are achievable
It bounds clock uncertainty with GPS/atomic clocks and waits out the uncertainty interval, managing rather than refuting the problem
It abandons physical time entirely and uses only Lamport timestamps internally
It ignores clock uncertainty and simply compares raw timestamps for speed
mcqs.explanation: TrueTime gives each node a bounded uncertainty interval [earliest, latest] and commit-waits until the interval has passed before assigning order. The uncertainty is real and paid for with added latency; TrueTime manages it, it does not eliminate or refute Lamport's underlying point.

topics.name: The Location-Transparency Fallacy: local calls are not remote calls
topics.premise: You can make a call to a remote object across a network look, in source code, exactly like a call to an object sitting in the same process. This convenience is a trap: the two are irreducibly different, and any abstraction that hides the difference smuggles false assumptions into every line that uses it. The network cannot be made 'just like local,' and pretending otherwise produces systems that are either unusably slow or silently broken.
topics.year: Jim Waldo, Geoff Wyant, Ann Wollrath, and Sam Kendall published 'A Note on Distributed Computing' at Sun Microsystems Labs in 1994 (TR-94-29, widely reprinted 1996), exactly as RPC, CORBA, and Java-RMI were promising that remote objects could be programmed the same way as local ones. It is the general principle behind this whole collection: a primitive's hidden assumptions are its undoing when the context changes — and it is precisely why STDIO, a same-host mechanism, cannot be transparently swapped in for cross-host communication.

prerequisites.explain:
Every running program (a process) is handed its own private range of memory addresses called its `address space`. Inside it, every object, variable, and function lives at some numeric address. A `pointer` (or reference) is simply one of those addresses stored as a value — a way to say 'the thing I mean is over there at address 0x7ffe...'.

The crucial property is that a pointer is only meaningful *inside the address space it came from*. Address 0x7ffe1234 in process A points to A's data; the very same number in process B points to something completely unrelated, or to nothing at all. There is no shared numbering scheme across processes, and certainly not across machines.

This is the bedrock for everything below. When two objects live in the same address space, one can hand the other a pointer and they instantly share the identical bytes — no copying, no encoding. The moment a boundary (another process, another machine) sits between them, pointers become gibberish and the whole comfortable model collapses.

A `procedure call` (or `method call` in object terms) is the fundamental unit of structured programming: you name a routine, hand it arguments, it runs, and it returns a value. Locally this is astonishingly cheap — the CPU pushes arguments and a return address onto the stack, jumps to the routine's code, runs it, and jumps back. It costs on the order of nanoseconds.

Two properties matter enormously and are usually invisible because they are always true. First, arguments can be `pointers`: `list.add(&item)` passes the address of `item`, and the callee sees the exact same object the caller has — mutations are shared for free. Second, caller and callee share fate. They run in one process; if the callee corrupts memory or the process is killed, *both* die together. There is no scenario where the caller keeps running while wondering whether the callee half-executed.

That combination — pointer passing plus shared fate plus near-zero latency — is what makes local calls feel like a single, atomic, reliable act. It is exactly this feel that RPC tried to reproduce over a network, and exactly what the network cannot deliver.

Since a pointer is worthless across a boundary, to send an argument to another process or machine you must convert the object into a self-contained sequence of bytes that carries the *values* themselves, not addresses. That conversion is called `marshalling` or `serialization`; the reverse — rebuilding an object on the far side from those bytes — is `unmarshalling` or `deserialization`.

This is fundamentally a *copy*, not a share. If you marshal a `Customer` object, send it, and the remote side mutates its copy, your original is untouched — the two objects are now independent. Cyclic graphs, shared sub-objects, and object identity all have to be encoded explicitly or lost. Large structures cost real time and bandwidth to encode, ship, and decode.

Marshalling is the concrete mechanism that makes 'memory access' differ between local and remote. It is not an implementation detail you can wave away: the semantics of your program change (copy vs. share), and a cost that was zero locally becomes proportional to the size of your data.

prerequisites.term: RPC / RMI / CORBA and the transparency goal
prerequisites.explain:
`Remote Procedure Call` (RPC) — and its object-oriented descendants Java `RMI` and `CORBA` — is the idea that calling a routine on another machine should look, in your source code, identical to calling one locally: `account.withdraw(100)` regardless of whether `account` is in your process or across the planet. The machinery that pulls this off is a `stub` (a local stand-in object) and a `skeleton` on the far side; the stub marshals the arguments, sends them over the network, waits, and unmarshals the reply, so the call *appears* synchronous and ordinary.

The explicit selling point was `location transparency`: the programmer shouldn't have to know or care where the object lives. Write your objects normally, flip a switch, and some of them become remote. This was genuinely seductive because the *syntax* really can be made identical.

Waldo et al.'s central claim is that this transparency is a fallacy. The syntax can be unified, but the *semantics* cannot — latency, memory access, partial failure, and concurrency all differ so fundamentally that hiding the boundary just means the differences ambush you later, at runtime, in production. The fix is not better plumbing; it is refusing to hide the boundary at all.

`Latency` is the time between issuing a call and getting the result. For a local method call this is single-digit nanoseconds. For a remote call it involves marshalling, an OS network stack, physical transmission (bounded by the speed of light — roughly 1 ms per 100 km of fiber, one way), queuing, the remote work, and the whole return trip.

A useful mental model: if a local call is one second, a same-datacenter round trip is on the order of days, and a cross-continent one is on the order of years. Concretely, remote calls are typically 4–5+ *orders of magnitude* slower than local ones — nanoseconds versus milliseconds.

This is why 'correct' code built on location transparency can still be unusable. A loop that calls `getName()` a million times is trivial locally and catastrophic remotely. You cannot sprinkle remote calls the way you sprinkle local ones; you must design coarse-grained interfaces that do a lot per round trip. Latency is not a tuning problem; it is a design constraint that must be visible in the interface.

In a single process, failure is `total`: either the call completes, or the whole program crashes and takes caller and callee with it. There is no in-between state where one half is alive and confused about the other. This shared fate is why local code rarely worries about 'what if the callee vanished mid-call.'

In a distributed system, the parts fail `independently`. The remote machine can crash while your machine runs on. The network can drop packets. A router can partition the two halves so each is healthy but cannot reach the other. There is no global 'off switch' that stops everyone at once.

The most vicious consequence is ambiguity. When a remote call times out, you genuinely cannot tell which of these happened: (a) the request never arrived and nothing was done, (b) it arrived, executed, and the *reply* was lost, or (c) it is still running. 'Didn't happen' and 'happened but I never heard back' are indistinguishable from the caller's side. This single fact — not latency — is the deepest reason remote objects must be programmed differently, and it forces concepts like timeouts, retries, and idempotency into your design whether you wanted them or not.

topics.why: Local and remote calls differ irreducibly along four axes: latency (nanoseconds vs. milliseconds — 4–5+ orders of magnitude), memory access (share a pointer vs. marshal a copy), partial failure (shared fate vs. independent failure with 'didn't happen vs. reply lost' ambiguity), and concurrency (one caller with a lock manager vs. many uncoordinated callers). Any abstraction that makes a remote call *look* like a local one necessarily hides these differences. Hidden differences do not go away — they resurface at runtime as systems that are unusably slow, silently inconsistent, or unable to reason about whether their own operations happened.
topics.deepDive:
Start from what a call actually is when both parties share one address space. You push arguments onto the stack, jump to the callee's code, and jump back with a result. Arguments can be pointers, so the callee operates on the very same bytes the caller holds — mutations are shared instantly and for free. The whole thing costs nanoseconds. And caller and callee share fate: they are one process, so either the call returns or the process dies and takes both of them down together. There is no third outcome. This trio — pointer sharing, near-zero latency, shared fate — is why a local call feels atomic and trustworthy. You almost never write code that asks 'did that call maybe half-happen?' because it can't.

RPC, and its object flavors RMI and CORBA, set out to reproduce that feel across a network. A local `stub` object stands in for the remote one; when you call it, the stub marshals your arguments into bytes, ships them, waits, and hands you back the unmarshalled reply. Syntactically, `account.withdraw(100)` looks the same whether `account` is next door or overseas. This was branded `location transparency`, and it was pitched as pure upside: write ordinary objects, decide later which ones live remotely, change nothing else. The seduction is real — because the *syntax* genuinely can be unified.

Waldo, Wyant, Wollrath, and Kendall's contribution in 'A Note on Distributed Computing' was to insist that unifying the syntax does nothing about the *semantics*, and the semantics are where distribution lives. Distributed objects, they argued, 'must be dealt with in ways that are intrinsically different from objects that interact in a single address space,' and it is a mistake to build systems that 'attempt to paper over the distinction between local and remote objects.' They laid out four axes on which the difference is not a matter of degree but of kind.

The first is latency. A local call is nanoseconds; a remote call is milliseconds or more — four to five-plus orders of magnitude slower. If a local call took one second, a datacenter round trip would take days. Code that is correct under location transparency can therefore be completely unusable: a fine-grained interface with a million tiny getters is instant locally and hours-long remotely. You cannot fix this by tuning; you have to design coarse-grained, batch-oriented interfaces, and that design decision has to be *visible* precisely where transparency tries to hide it.

The second is memory access. Locally you pass a pointer and share the object. Remotely there is no shared address space, so a pointer — just a number meaningful only in its home process — is worthless across the boundary. You must `marshal` the object into self-contained bytes and send a *copy*. That changes semantics, not just performance: mutate the copy on the far side and your original is untouched; object identity, shared sub-objects, and cyclic graphs must be explicitly encoded or silently lost. 'Pass by reference' and 'pass by copy' are different programs, and transparency papers over which one you're actually getting.

The third, and the one the authors treat as central, is partial failure. Locally, failure is total and shared: the whole process lives or dies as one. Remotely, the parts fail independently — the remote node can crash while you run on, the network can drop your packet, a partition can leave both sides healthy but unable to talk. Worse than the failure itself is the ambiguity it creates: when a call times out, you cannot distinguish 'the request never arrived and nothing happened' from 'it executed but the reply was lost' from 'it's still running.' A local call never leaves you in that fog. This is why remoteness cannot be hidden: the caller must be given a way to *reason about not knowing*, which local semantics never had to express.

The fourth is concurrency. A local object typically fields calls in a controlled way, with a shared lock manager and a single consistent view of ordering available to the whole process. A remote object is hit by many independent clients at once, with no shared lock manager and no single global clock, so there is no one canonical ordering of events. Correctness arguments that quietly relied on 'only one thing at a time, in a knowable order' evaporate.

Two later formulations sharpen the same lesson. Martin Fowler's 'First Law of Distributed Object Design' is blunt: 'don't distribute your objects' — because turning an in-process object graph into a network of remote objects imports all four problems for what is usually no real benefit; distribute at coarse service boundaries you actually need, not at every object. And the 'Fallacies of Distributed Computing' enumerate eight false assumptions that location-transparent code silently bakes in: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous. Each fallacy is exactly one of the truths that transparency hides until it bites.

The payoff is not 'never build distributed systems' — that would be absurd. It is: don't *hide* the distribution; make it explicit in the interface. Expect failure and design for it (timeouts, retries, idempotency so a retried call is safe). Design for latency with coarse-grained, batched calls. Copy rather than share, and be honest about the copy. Distribute only where you must. In short, let the boundary show, because the boundary is real.

And this is exactly the general law behind the whole collection. STDIO is a same-host mechanism: two processes on one machine, wired by pipes, sharing fate under one operating system, exchanging bytes at effectively zero latency with no independent partial failure between them. Every one of those is a hidden assumption. Try to swap STDIO transparently for cross-host communication and each assumption breaks — latency appears, fate becomes independent, 'the other end just vanished' becomes a real state you must handle. A primitive's hidden assumptions are its undoing when the context changes, and location transparency is the purest statement of why.

solutions: Make remoteness explicit in the interface

Do not disguise a network call as a local one. A remote-capable interface should announce, in its type or signature, that it can fail, take real time, and return copies rather than shared references. Prefer coarse-grained operations that do meaningful work per round trip over chatty fine-grained getters. When the caller can see that a boundary is being crossed, they write code that respects it; when the boundary is hidden, they write code that assumes it away.
Design for partial failure (timeouts, retries, idempotency)

Assume every remote call can time out in the ambiguous state where you cannot tell 'didn't happen' from 'happened but the reply was lost.' Give every call a bounded timeout, decide a retry policy, and — critically — make operations idempotent so that a retried call that actually did execute the first time causes no double effect (e.g., use request IDs or conditional writes). This is not optional hardening; it is the core semantic difference between local and remote, made into design.
Copy, don't share — marshal data across the boundary

There is no shared address space across machines, so stop thinking in pointers at the boundary. Explicitly serialize the values you send, accept that the far side gets an independent copy, and design your data so it is self-contained and cheap to encode. Be deliberate about object identity, shared sub-structures, and large payloads, because each has real bandwidth and latency cost and none of the free sharing you enjoyed locally.
Don't distribute objects you don't have to (Fowler's First Law)

The best way to survive the four axes is to cross the network as rarely as possible. Keep collaborating objects in one process where you can, and introduce a network boundary only at deliberate, coarse service seams that you actually need for scaling, isolation, or ownership reasons. Fewer remote calls means fewer places where latency, copying, partial failure, and uncoordinated concurrency can hurt you.

topics.takeaway: You can make a remote call look like a local call, but you cannot make it behave like one — latency, copying, partial failure, and concurrency are differences of kind, not degree. Don't hide the network; make it visible in your interfaces and design for the boundary you're actually crossing.

mcqs.q: According to Waldo et al., what is the fundamental error that RPC/CORBA/RMI 'location transparency' makes?
options: It uses the wrong wire format for serializing objects
It papers over the distinction between local and remote objects, hiding differences that are differences of kind, not degree
It makes remote calls too explicit, cluttering the code
It forbids passing any arguments to remote methods
mcqs.explanation: The paper's thesis is that remote objects 'must be dealt with in ways that are intrinsically different' and that it is a mistake to 'paper over the distinction' between local and remote. Unifying the syntax leaves the semantics irreducibly different.

mcqs.q: A client sends a remote request and the call times out. What can the client reliably conclude?
options: The operation definitely did not happen
The operation definitely happened but the reply was lost
Nothing definite — it may not have happened, may have happened with the reply lost, or may still be running
The remote machine has permanently crashed
mcqs.explanation: This is the core partial-failure ambiguity. A timeout cannot distinguish 'never arrived / nothing done' from 'executed but reply lost' from 'still running.' Local calls never leave you in this fog because of shared fate.

mcqs.q: Why can't you pass a pointer to a remote object and have it work the way it does locally?
options: Pointers are too large to send over a network
A pointer is an address meaningful only within its own process's address space; there is no shared address space across the boundary, so you must marshal a copy
Remote objects don't have memory
Network protocols strip out pointer values for security
mcqs.explanation: A pointer is just a number meaningful inside one address space. Across processes/machines there is no shared address space, so the object must be marshalled (serialized) into self-contained bytes and sent as a copy — with different mutation semantics.

mcqs.q: Roughly how much slower is a typical remote call than a local method call, per the paper's framing?
options: About 2x slower
About 10x slower
About 4–5 or more orders of magnitude slower
Remote calls are usually faster due to dedicated hardware
mcqs.explanation: A local call is nanoseconds; a remote call is milliseconds or more — 4 to 5+ orders of magnitude. This is why location-transparent code can be perfectly correct yet completely unusable, and why coarse-grained interfaces matter.

mcqs.q: What is the correct lesson of the location-transparency fallacy?
options: Never build distributed systems
Always distribute every object for maximum scalability
Don't hide the distribution — make remoteness explicit and design for latency, copying, and partial failure
Use a faster network so remote calls behave like local ones
mcqs.explanation: The fix is not to avoid distribution but to stop hiding it. Make the boundary visible in the interface, expect failure (timeouts/retries/idempotency), copy rather than share, and — per Fowler — don't distribute objects you don't have to.

mcqs.q: How does the location-transparency fallacy explain why STDIO can't be transparently swapped for cross-host communication?
options: STDIO is too slow even on the same host
STDIO's hidden assumptions — same host, shared fate, zero latency, no independent partial failure — all break once a network boundary is introduced
STDIO cannot transmit binary data
Cross-host communication is always faster than STDIO
mcqs.explanation: STDIO is a same-host, shared-fate, near-instant mechanism. Each of those is a hidden assumption. Substituting it across hosts introduces latency, independent failure, and the 'did it happen?' ambiguity — the general law that a primitive's hidden assumptions undo it when the context changes.
